\documentclass{article}
\title{Learning Dynamics in Repeated Cournot Competition}
\author{G. Papadakis}
\date{July 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\section{Introduction}
Firms that repeatedly compete in quantities
face a tension between short-term undercutting and long-term coordination.
We study how simple learning rules shape the outcomes of this interaction
when players observe only their own profits and the market price.

\section{Related Work}
The classical analysis of quantity competition focuses on static equilibria.
Learning in games has been studied extensively for finite games,
but continuous action spaces with quadratic payoffs
offer a tractable middle ground with rich dynamics.

\section{Model}
Two firms choose quantities in each period.
The market price is linear in total supply,
and production costs are quadratic.
Each firm updates its quantity by a no-regret rule
driven by the profit gradient estimated from past play.

\section{Convergence}
For small step sizes the joint dynamics converge
to a neighbourhood of the Nash equilibrium.
Larger step sizes lead to persistent cycles,
and beyond a threshold the dynamics become chaotic.
The boundary between these regimes can be characterised in closed form.

\section{Collusion}
When both firms use gradient estimates with long memory,
the dynamics drift toward the collusive outcome instead.
Memory effectively gives each firm a coarse model of the other,
which is enough to sustain tacit coordination without any communication.

\section{Welfare}
Total surplus in the cyclic regime is lower than at the Nash equilibrium,
while the collusive regime transfers surplus from consumers to firms.
The results suggest that the design of learning algorithms
has first-order welfare consequences in automated markets.

\section{Extensions}
Allowing entry by a third firm destabilises the collusive regime,
and the dynamics settle into a three-player cycle instead.
Capacity constraints soften the chaotic regime
by limiting how aggressively either firm can expand output.

\section{Conclusion}
Simple learning rules generate rich dynamics in repeated quantity competition,
and small changes in memory length move the market between regimes.
\end{document}
